papers.title: The Long March to Innovation: R&D and Competitive Evolution in the Indian Pharmaceutical Industry
papers.abstract: TRIPS (1995) has played a major role in shaping the Indian pharmaceutical industry. Conventional theory suggests that strong intellectual property rights (IPR) frameworks should strengthen innovation incentives. Yet, two decades after TRIPS, growth in India’s novel innovation pipeline has stalled. This chapter challenges the assumption that stronger IPR alone would catalyze discovery-based R&D. We utilize trial phase transition data from the Biomedtracker database, finding that the Indian pipeline faces a bottleneck in transitioning clinical trials specifically from Phase 1 to Phase 2, supported by a null result in transitions from Phase 1 to Phase 3, benchmarked against China and the United Kingdom. We argue that this reflects binding constraints in the Indian ecosystem that are likely orthogonal to IPR, accompanied by a within-firm shift toward non-novel programs. We corroborate these arguments through interviews with Indian pharmaceutical industry experts. Our findings should inform thinking about normative IPR in developing economies.

papers.title: The Why and How of Foreign Aid
papers.abstract: Foreign aid has become a melting pot of motivations and policies, where differently-motivated actors often converge on recommended policies while the similarly-motivated diverge. Breaking down the “why” and the “how” can illuminate real tensions and reveal false ones. The “why” asks which problems to tackle and who benefits: the recipient, the donor through economic, political, or soft-power returns, or everyone through global public goods. The “how” asks which strategy most cost-effectively addresses a chosen problem. Evidence is central to the “how”: use it where it exists, produce it where it does not. In particular, approaches which improve state capacity to use and generate evidence can satisfy multiple objectives: strengthen recipient countries, benefit donors, and provide a global public good of knowledge. Ultimately, the “how” is not a linear process, but rather an iterative one of learning, adopting, adapting, repeating, and then sharing so others can learn as well.

papers.title: Foreign Giants' Broad Shoulders: The Causal Effect of Foreign Ideas on U.S. Innovation
papers.abstract: We study the role of foreign ideas in U.S. innovation by constructing a directed “genealogy” of technologies from the full text of 13 million patents filed between 1887 and 2024. By tracing which earlier technologies appear in the founding patents of new ones, we recover a large-scale input–output network of technological recombination that identifies the foreign technologies that serve as inputs into innovation in the United States. We report four main findings. First, foreign ideas are pervasive: 54% of U.S. technologies build on at least one foreign input, and the most fertile U.S. technologies rely on foreign inputs most heavily. Second, foreign ideas have large causal effects on U.S. innovation. Using the historical settlement of migrants as a source of exogenous variation in local ancestry, we show that U.S. counties more exposed to knowledge from a given foreign country absorb substantially more technologies from that country and, in turn, invent significantly more U.S. technologies building on them. Third, foreign ideas shape not only the level but also the direction of technical change: U.S. counties are far more likely to pioneer the specific technologies whose foreign inputs are already in their local idea stock, and the changing origins of foreign ideas accompany the shift of American innovation from its historical heartland toward the coasts. Fourth, these effects leave a lasting imprint on local labor markets: decades later, counties that absorbed more of an origin’s ideas host more jobs working with those ideas, and even more work with the U.S. technologies descended from them.

papers.title: Credit Markets with New Screening Technologies
papers.abstract: We study equilibrium market structure in a model of credit-market competition with correlated or uncorrelated screening errors and endogenous screening technologies. A pool externality arises because rejected borrowers reapply elsewhere, so lenders’ screening and pricing choices affect competitors’ applicant pools. With independent errors, a single market segment emerges, with rates rising smoothly as lenders who choose better technologies lend to more adversely selected borrowers. With correlated screening errors, potentially stemming from similar AI systems and overlapping financial-sector data, ex-ante identical lenders instead specialize across qualitatively distinct segments, generating a hockey-stick interest-rate schedule: segments with uniform rates but heterogeneous borrower quality coexist with segments featuring uniform quality but dispersed rates, echoing traditional banking, fintech, and high-rate indiscriminate lending. We show how technological and regulatory changes affecting screening costs, including frontier AI innovation and various forms of open banking, unevenly affect financial access and can either benefit or harm financially excluded borrowers.

papers.title: Green Subsidies with Demand Distortions
papers.abstract: Credit constraints and other demand distortions are pervasive in lower-income contexts. A model of clean technology adoption shows that demand distortions can increase the welfare gains from green subsidies. This arises through two channels: shifting the marginal adopter toward higher private and social benefits, and increasing demand elasticity. We test this by cross-randomizing purchase price subsidies, usage subsidies, and access to an interest-free loan for a US$84 induction stove among 2,134 charcoal users in Kenya. Usage subsidies of 75% have a precise zero effect on adoption and usage. Purchase price subsidies, however, generate large welfare gains. Credit constraints raise the subsidy’s efficacy by 35%–73%, up to US$10–US$12 in observable welfare gain per subsidy dollar. This demand distortion also lowers the subsidy cost of abatement by 41%, to US$12 per tCO2e. This operates through the two channels identified in the theory: credit constraints raise the marginal adopter’s positive externality by 19% and fuel savings by 30%, and lower the subsidy cost per marginal adoption by 29%. In a counterfactual without demand distortions, the abatement cost rises to US$137 per tCO2e. Contexts with large demand distortions could offer many cost-effective opportunities for climate change mitigation financing.

papers.title: Upgrading Financial Markets
papers.abstract: Expanding access to financial services may not be enough to develop markets in low-income settings: providers also need to be held accountable to consumers. We test this in a field experiment across 195 rural Sierra Leonean communities, upgrading Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLAs) into mobile money and bank agents, cross-randomized with a monthly consumer feedback mechanism. Upgrading expands access, but feedback drives large operational improvements (+20.5 pp, 85%), particularly in privacy and consumer protection, raising usage and revenues. Upgraded VSLAs also show higher savings digitization and higher incomes, evidence that disciplining agent actions benefits not only consumers but also the principal that finances and stands behind its agent. Interpreted through a framework of delegated intermediation, we show accountability, not infrastructure alone, aligns provider incentives with consumer welfare and is central to designing scalable financial intermediaries.
